body:
**Child abduction and organ trafficking: what parents should do?**

Child abduction and rumours of organ trafficking are major worries for parents. The purpose of this article is to help parents stay calm and have specific steps to take when needed — no sensationalism, no alarmism, no premature conclusions. This article summarises Vietnamese law, warning signs, what to do in the first 60 minutes, and when to call 111 or 113.

## Your child is late: what to do right now?

Do not wait until tomorrow. Call 113 (Police Rapid Response) and 111 (National Child Protection Hotline) right away, describing your child, the last time you saw them, and the last place you met. Both lines are free and operate 24/7.

## What is child abduction under Vietnamese law?

Under the 2015 Penal Code (amended 2017), abducting or detaining a child under 16 by force, threat, or other means is the crime of taking custody of a person under 16, set out in Article 153, punishable by 3 to 7 years in prison.

## Organ trafficking: what is confirmed and what is rumour?

Vietnamese law defines the crime of buying, selling, or taking custody of human organs or body parts in Article 154 (3 to 7 years, higher in serious cases). No official source confirms cases of children abducted to harvest organs in Vietnam.

## Warning signs that a child may be at risk of abduction

These warning signs help parents spot child abduction risk early and act quickly. A single sign does not necessarily mean a child is in danger, but several signs appearing together warrant closer attention and checking with the child or contacting authorities.


| Warning sign | What to do |
|---|---|
| Child does not return at the agreed time without notice | Call 113 and 111 immediately, give full details |
| Strangers frequently appearing near home or school | Note characteristics, driver, licence plate |
| Child walking alone in isolated areas | Remind the child to go in groups and not get into strangers’ vehicles |
| Child accepting gifts or invitations from strangers | Ask the child, encourage them to speak up |
| Child becomes fearful or secretive around one person | Talk with the child; seek psychological support if needed |

The table lists general warning signs and does not treat any specific person as a criminal without clear grounds.

## The first 60 minutes: what to do if your child goes missing

If you suspect your child is missing, every minute counts. Act immediately: call 113 to report to Police Rapid Response, call 111 for the National Child Protection Hotline, give a full description, and contact the school, friends, and neighbours to check.

1. Call 113 to report the case to the Police Rapid Response.
2. Call 111 to be supported and counselled by the National Child Protection Hotline.
3. Give a full description: age, clothing, identifying features, last place seen.
4. Contact the school, friends, and neighbours to check whether the child has appeared.
5. Stay calm so you can give clear information and help the authorities act quickly.

Acting fast in the first 60 minutes increases the chance of finding your child. Do not let panic delay your report.

![Checklist for the first 60 minutes if a child goes missing](/static/img/articles/child-safety-60-minutes.svg)

## How does Vietnamese law handle abduction and human trafficking?

Under the 2015 Penal Code (amended 2017), abduction and trafficking are prosecuted under Articles 150, 153 and 154. Penalties range from 3 to 20 years, or life imprisonment in aggravated cases. No official source has confirmed organ trafficking in Vietnam.

Under the 2015 Penal Code (amended 2017), legal lookup site:

- **Article 150 — Crime of trafficking in people:** using force, threat, deception, or other means to transfer or receive a person in exchange for money, property, or benefits, or for sexual exploitation, forced labour, or taking the victim’s body parts. Punishable by 5 to 10 years in prison; if body parts have already been taken from the victim, the range rises to 12 to 20 years.
- **Article 153 — Crime of taking custody of a person under 16:** detaining or handing over a child under 16 to another person for detention by force, threat, or other means. Punishable by 3 to 7 years, higher if organised or if a position is abused.
- **Article 154 — Crime of buying, selling, or taking custody of human organs or body parts:** punishable by 3 to 7 years; serious cases (professional, causing death, six or more people) are punishable by 12 to 20 years or life imprisonment.

## Recent high-profile cases: what is true?

Several rumours about child abduction and organ trafficking have spread widely on social media recently. Below is what the authorities have announced, and what remains a rumour.

**1. Can Tho (23/09/2026):** A rumour about child abduction in the Ninh Kieu district spread on social media. Ninh Kieu ward police (Can Tho) investigated and announced: the information is completely untrue; the story originated from a child’s imagination, and no incident occurred.

**2. Thai Nguyen (25/06/2026):** A post about a mother and child being abducted in Quyên Thánh ward caused alarm on social media. Thai Nguyen provincial police said the information was unverified, and preliminary findings showed no signs of abduction.

**3. Nghe An (16/04/2025):** Two women posted unverified abduction information on social media. Nghe An police fined each woman 7.5 million VND for providing false information that caused public alarm.

**4. Tra Vinh (03/11/2024):** The investigating police of Chau Thanh district (Tra Vinh province) prosecuted the case and detained a woman for kidnapping a newborn at a hospital. This article does not name the accused.

### How to check a rumour in 60 seconds

1. Do not share immediately when you see a sensational post about child abduction.
2. Look for information on the official website of the local police before believing it.
3. Call 113 or 111 to confirm before acting.
4. No official announcement? Treat as rumour; do not share.

## How can parents prevent this in everyday life?

Prevention starts with regular conversation between parents and children, not only when something happens. Families should agree on times, places and who the child will meet, and teach basic safety rules for walking alone, accepting gifts, or getting into strangers' vehicles.

Prevention starts with regular conversation, not only when something happens:

- Agree on the time and place your child will be, and ask them to tell you if plans change.
- Teach your child not to walk alone in isolated areas, not to accept gifts, and not to get into strangers’ vehicles.
- Set up safe zones on the map and receive alerts when your child arrives at or leaves them.
- Encourage your child to share their location when needed, with a time limit (for example, stopping automatically after 60 minutes) to respect privacy.
- Make clear to your child who the trusted people are to call in an emergency.
- Avoid posting photos, names, schools, or detailed addresses of your child on public networks.

![Family safe zones: home, school, park](/static/img/articles/child-safety-safezone.svg)

## Things NOT to do if your child goes missing

- Do not wait until tomorrow; time is precious in the first 60 minutes.
- Do not share unverified rumours before authorities confirm.
- Do not confront suspects; let police handle it.
- Do not post your child's personal details publicly while searching.

## When should you call 111 or 113?

Call 113 when a crime is happening, someone is in danger, or there are signs of an offence. Call 111 when you need advice and urgent help for children, including cases related to human trafficking and exploitation. Both lines operate 24/7.

## Frequently asked questions (FAQ)

**Can rumours about organ trafficking be trusted?**

No official source has confirmed this in Vietnam. Wait for the authorities.

**Your child is missing — who do you call first?**

Call 113 (police) first, then 111 (National Child Protection Hotline) for support.

**Does Kigo prevent abduction?**

No. Kigo supports safe-zone alerts and location sharing chosen by the child, but it does not replace the police and does not claim to prevent abduction.

**Does my child have the right not to share location?**

Yes. Location is shared only if the child agrees and stops automatically after 60 minutes.

**How many guardians can be linked?**

Up to 3 guardians per child under Kigo’s design.

**Is Kigo available on Android?**

No. Kigo (international name: FamHub) is available on the App Store; Android is not yet on Google Play.

**Is it safe to post photos of my child online?**

It is better to avoid posting photos, names, schools, or detailed addresses of your child on public networks, to protect their privacy and safety.
